lead: The 8086 has one mode pin, MN/MX. Tie it high and the CPU drives the system control bus itself; tie it low and the CPU hands status to an external 8288 bus controller. This choice decides whether a board is a small single-processor system or a larger system with bus masters and coprocessors. The same address latches and data transceivers are used in both modes. The mode changes which pins carry ALE, DEN, DT/R, RD and WR, so read every pin name together with its mode.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for 8086 signals and the BIU, and Chapter 2.2 for T-states and bus timing.

sections.h3: One pin selects the control source

blocks.text: MN/MX is pin 33. A high level (+5 V) selects minimum mode. A low level (0 V) selects maximum mode. The pin does not change the instruction set or registers. It changes the control pins on the right side of the chip.

In minimum mode the 8086 itself drives the control bus. It produces RD, WR, M/IO, ALE, DEN, DT/R and INTA. It accepts HOLD and returns HLDA. One processor owns the bus, so no bus controller is needed.

In maximum mode the same pins carry different signals. The 8086 sends status S2, S1, S0, queue status QS1, QS0, LOCK, RQ/GT1 and RQ/GT0. It does not drive RD or WR. An external 8288 bus controller decodes S2-S0 into memory and I/O commands. The 8288 also produces ALE, DEN and DT/R. Maximum mode exists for systems with a coprocessor, a DMA controller, or more than one bus master. Minimum mode is cheaper for a small single-processor board.

Tie MN/MX to +5 V. The 8284 clock generator supplies CLK, READY and RESET to the 8086. A crystal connects to the 8284; it divides the crystal frequency and gives a clean clock. READY inserts wait states for slow memory. RESET starts the CPU.

The address bus needs latches. AD0-AD15 carry both address bits A0-A15 and data bits D0-D15. A16-A19 share pins with status S3-S6. ALE is high at the start of a bus cycle. An 8282 latch (two chips for the 16 lower address bits, one for A16-A19 and BHE) stores the address on the falling edge of ALE. The address stays stable while the same pins carry data later in the cycle. See Chapter 2.2 for the T-states.

The data bus needs a transceiver. Two 8286 chips buffer D0-D15. DEN enables the buffer. DT/R sets direction: high for transmit (CPU to memory), low for receive (memory to CPU). The 8086 drives M/IO to select memory or I/O, and RD or WR to set the direction of the transfer. Memory and I/O chips connect to the latched address, the buffered data bus, and these control lines.

HOLD and HLDA allow bus sharing. A DMA controller raises HOLD. The 8086 floats its buses and raises HLDA. The DMA controller then uses the bus. Minimum mode is used in small trainer kits and simple single-board systems.

sections.h3: Maximum mode system and status decoding

blocks.text: Tie MN/MX to 0 V. The 8086 sends S2-S0 to the 8288. The 8288 decodes the three bits into active-low bus commands. It also uses CLK and AEN; AEN can force the command outputs to a known state when another master owns the bus.

The 8288 produces MRDC, MWTC, IORC, IOWC, INTA and AMWC. It also produces ALE, DEN and DT/R for the 8282 latches and 8286 transceivers. The address and data path is the same as in minimum mode; only the source of control changes.

Queue status QS1-QS0 tells what the BIU is doing: no operation, first byte of the queue, empty queue, or later byte. LOCK prevents another bus master from taking the bus during a locked instruction. RQ/GT0 and RQ/GT1 let another master request and receive the bus. Maximum mode is used with the 8087 numeric coprocessor, the 8089 I/O processor, and multiprocessor boards.
Some syllabi call these “min mode system configuration” and “max mode system configuration”. The choice is wiring, not software: the same 8086 runs the same instructions in either mode.

A small board with one CPU and ordinary memory uses minimum mode: fewer chips, direct control, lower cost. A board with a coprocessor, a DMA controller that must become bus master, or two processors uses maximum mode: the 8288 gives standard commands and the RQ/GT pins arbitrate the bus. A common exam mistake is to place an 8288 on a minimum-mode board or to look for RD and WR from the 8086 in maximum mode.

figure.caption: The 8086 uses the 8284 clock, 8282 address latches and 8286 data transceivers in both modes; the 8288 is present only in maximum mode, where it drives the control bus from S2-S0.

spec.title: 8086 minimum and maximum mode
spec.aria: The 8086 uses the 8284 clock, 8282 latches and 8286 transceivers in both modes; in maximum mode it sends status S2-S0 to the 8288 bus controller, which drives the control bus, while in minimum mode the 8086 drives control directly.

examples.question: In a maximum-mode 8086 system the status lines are S2 S1 S0 = 101. Which 8288 output is active, and what bus operation does it perform?
steps: MN/MX is low, so the 8086 is in maximum mode. It drives status bits S2, S1 and S0 to the 8288 bus controller.
Read the bits in the order S2 S1 S0: S2 = 1, S1 = 0, S0 = 1. The status code is binary 101, which is decimal 5.
In the 8288 status table, code 101 means a memory read. The 8288 asserts its MRDC (active-low memory read command) output.
The address comes from the 8282 latches, and the memory places data on D0-D15 for the 8086 to read.
examples.answer: MRDC (active low) is active, so the 8288 performs a memory read; the status code is decimal 5.
examples.check:
s2 = 1
s1 = 0
s0 = 1
status = (s2 << 2) | (s1 << 1) | s0
print(status)

traps: Learning pin names without the mode. ALE, DEN and DT/R are minimum-mode names; in maximum mode the same pins carry queue status and S2-S0, and the 8288 produces the control signals.
Thinking the 8288 generates the clock. The 8284 generates CLK, READY and RESET; the 8288 decodes S2-S0 into bus commands.
Connecting an 8288 in minimum mode or expecting RD and WR from the 8086 in maximum mode. Read the MN/MX level first, then choose the control source.
Reversing the status order. S2 S1 S0 = 101 is a memory read (MRDC); S2 S1 S0 = 110 is a memory write (MWTC).
Confusing the 8282 latch with the 8286 transceiver. The 8282 holds the address; the 8286 buffers the data and uses DEN and DT/R.

quiz.q: What does the MN/MX pin of the 8086 select?
quiz.a: It selects minimum mode when high (+5 V) and maximum mode when low (0 V).

quiz.q: Why does a maximum-mode 8086 system need an 8288 bus controller?
quiz.a: In maximum mode the 8086 does not drive RD and WR directly. It sends status S2-S0, and the 8288 decodes those bits into MRDC, MWTC, IORC, IOWC and INTA. The 8288 also gives ALE, DEN and DT/R for the latches and transceivers.

quiz.q: A maximum-mode 8086 sends S2 S1 S0 = 110. Which 8288 output is active, and what operation is performed?
quiz.a: Code 110 means memory write. The 8288 asserts MWTC (active low), so data is written from the 8086 to memory.

quiz.q: A student ties MN/MX high and also connects an 8288 to the 8086. Explain why this board will not work as intended.
quiz.a: MN/MX high selects minimum mode. In minimum mode the 8086 pins carry ALE, DEN, DT/R, RD and WR, not the status S2-S0 and queue status that the 8288 needs. The 8288 therefore gets no valid status and its control outputs are wrong. The 8288 belongs only in maximum mode.

quiz.q: Name two control signals produced by the 8086 in minimum mode but not produced by the 8086 in maximum mode.
quiz.a: Any two of RD, WR, M/IO, ALE, DEN, DT/R and INTA. In maximum mode these functions move to the 8288 or become status signals.

quiz.q: In a minimum-mode 8086 system, a DMA controller raises HOLD. What does the 8086 do?
quiz.a: The 8086 finishes its current bus cycle, floats its address, data and control buses, and raises HLDA. The DMA controller can then use the bus.

quiz.q: Why are 8282 latches needed when the 8086 already has address pins?
quiz.a: AD0-AD15 carry address and data at different times, and A16-A19 share pins with status. The address is valid only early in the bus cycle. ALE stores it in the 8282 latch so memory and I/O see a stable address while the same pins carry data later.

quiz.q: What are S2, S1 and S0 in a maximum-mode 8086 system?
quiz.a: They are the three status bits that tell the 8288 what bus operation the 8086 wants: interrupt acknowledge, I/O read, I/O write, halt, instruction fetch, memory read, memory write, or passive.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern x86 chips integrate the bus controller and memory controller on the same die, so the 8288 is a museum part. The idea survives as a bus bridge or memory controller that decodes a request type into read and write strobes. Bus arbitration appears today in AMBA AHB/APB and PCIe root complexes. Search “8086 maximum mode 8288 timing” and “bus arbiter RQ/GT” to go deeper.
